title: Orthodontics & IOTN
blurb: How malocclusion is assessed with IOTN, fixed, removable and functional appliances, retainers, and keeping teeth healthy in braces.
question: A 13-year-old attends an orthodontic assessment. The orthodontist records IOTN Dental Health Component 3 and Aesthetic Component 7, and plans fixed braces. Mum asks whether this is available on the NHS and what her son must do to keep his teeth healthy during treatment. What would you explain?

teach.body: Orthodontics corrects malocclusion: teeth that are crowded, spaced, rotated or sticking out, or jaws that don't meet properly. Treatment can improve function, make teeth easier to clean and improve appearance. Assessment involves a history, an examination, the IOTN score and records: study models or scans, photographs and radiographs such as a panoramic (OPT) or lateral cephalometric view. Dental nurses support this work and can gain the NEBDN Certificate in Orthodontic Dental Nursing.

teach.caption: The grade is set by the single worst feature found. Grade 5 examples: teeth unable to erupt, an overjet over 9 mm, cleft lip and palate.

teach.body: IOTN is the Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need. The Dental Health Component (DHC) grades the health risk of the malocclusion from 1 to 5. The Aesthetic Component (AC) compares the patient's front teeth with a scale of 10 photographs, from 1 (most attractive) to 10 (least). In England, NHS orthodontics for under-18s is usually available for DHC 4 or 5, or DHC 3 with an AC of 6 or more. So the boy in the scenario qualifies.

teach.caption: Fixed braces use brackets, an archwire and elastic modules or ligatures; molar bands are often cemented with glass ionomer. A Twin Block is a common functional appliance.
In severe crowding the orthodontist may ask for premolars to be extracted, often the first premolars (14, 24, 34, 44), before the braces close the spaces.

teach.h: Chairside at a fixed brace bond-up
items: Prepare cheek retractors, bracket holder, etch, bonding agent, adhesive, curing light and the archwires.
Polish the teeth, then keep them dry: aspiration and isolation matter as much as in any bonding procedure.
Etch, rinse and dry, then apply the bonding agent as the clinician directs.
Pass each bracket with adhesive in order; the clinician positions it and you help remove excess and cure.
Pass the archwire and elastic modules, then distal end cutters to trim the wire ends.
Give oral hygiene, diet and 'what to do if something breaks' advice, and book the next adjustment.

teach.body: Brackets trap plaque. Without good care the enamel round them decalcifies, leaving white spot lesions (early caries), and the gums become inflamed. Advise brushing thoroughly twice a day and after meals, angling the brush above and below the brackets, plus interdental or single-tufted brushes. Use fluoride toothpaste (1,350–1,500 ppm) and, if advised, a daily fluoride mouthrinse at a different time from brushing. Cut down sugary and fizzy drinks and avoid hard or sticky foods that break brackets.

teach.h: A typical course of fixed treatment

items.label: Retainers fitted
items.sub: Worn as advised, often long term

teach.body: Teeth tend to drift back towards where they started. Retainers hold them in their new position. Removable retainers can be clear vacuum-formed (Essix-type) or acrylic with wire (Hawley). A fixed (bonded) retainer is a thin wire bonded behind the front teeth. Patients are usually advised to keep wearing retainers for the long term, so explain how to clean them and to contact the practice if a bonded wire comes loose.

teach.text: Don't mix up the two IOTN parts. The Dental Health Component goes from 1 to 5 and measures health need; the Aesthetic Component goes from 1 to 10 and measures appearance. DHC 3 alone doesn't qualify for NHS treatment in England; DHC 3 needs an AC of 6 or more.

items: NHS (England, under 18): DHC 4 or 5, or DHC 3 with AC 6 or more.
Removable = tipping; fixed = all movements; functional = guide jaw growth.
Plaque round brackets causes white spot lesions and gingivitis: brush well, fluoride, cut sugar.
Retainers prevent relapse and are often worn long term.

summary: You can now explain IOTN and who qualifies for NHS orthodontics, compare removable, fixed and functional appliances, support the clinician at a bond-up, and give the oral hygiene and retainer advice that keeps braces patients' teeth healthy.

A.q: What does the Dental Health Component of IOTN measure?
options: How attractive the front teeth look
How much the malocclusion risks oral health
How long treatment is likely to take
How well the patient is likely to wear a brace
A.why: The DHC grades the health risk of the malocclusion from 1 (no need) to 5 (very great need).

whyNot.0: Appearance is measured by the Aesthetic Component.
whyNot.2: IOTN does not predict treatment length.
whyNot.3: Cooperation is assessed clinically; it isn't part of IOTN.

A.q: A patient's fixed brace has brackets bonded to every tooth with an archwire. What kind of tooth movement can it achieve that a simple removable appliance cannot?
options: Guiding the lower jaw forward during growth
A.why: Fixed appliances can move teeth bodily, rotate them and control root position, not just tip crowns.

whyNot.0: Tipping is what simple removable appliances do.
whyNot.1: Holding teeth after treatment is the job of retainers.
whyNot.3: Guiding jaw growth is what functional appliances are designed for.

A.q: A patient in fixed braces has chalky white marks round several brackets. What are these most likely to be?
options: Leftover bonding adhesive round the brackets
A.why: Plaque trapped round brackets demineralises enamel, causing white spot lesions, the earliest stage of caries.

whyNot.0: Tea and coffee cause brown staining, not chalky white patches round brackets.
whyNot.1: Fluorosis happens while teeth develop and isn't linked to bracket position.
whyNot.2: Excess adhesive is removed at bonding and doesn't appear as chalky enamel.

B.q: A 14-year-old in England has IOTN DHC grade 3. Which Aesthetic Component score would make them eligible for NHS orthodontics?
B.why: DHC 3 qualifies for NHS treatment when the Aesthetic Component is 6 or more.

whyNot.0: AC 2 is well below the threshold of 6.
whyNot.1: AC 4 is below the threshold of 6.
whyNot.3: AC 5 is just below the threshold of 6.

B.q: A growing 11-year-old with a large overjet and a short lower jaw is given a Twin Block. What type of appliance is this?
B.why: A Twin Block is a functional appliance that holds the lower jaw forward to use growth to correct a Class II pattern.

whyNot.0: Fixed appliances use bonded brackets and wires.
whyNot.1: A vacuum-formed retainer holds teeth in place after treatment; it doesn't guide growth.
whyNot.2: A bonded retainer is a wire fixed behind the teeth after treatment.

B.q: Which advice is most appropriate for a patient who has just had fixed braces fitted?
options: Brush only once a day to protect the brackets
Use interdental brushes and fluoride toothpaste
Rinse with water instead of brushing near wires
Chew hard foods to help the teeth move faster
B.why: Interdental brushes clean round brackets and under wires, and fluoride protects enamel from decalcification.

whyNot.0: Braces need more cleaning, not less: twice a day and after meals.
whyNot.2: Water alone does not remove plaque from brackets.
whyNot.3: Hard foods break brackets and don't speed treatment.

C.q: Which grade of the IOTN Dental Health Component means a very great need for treatment?
C.why: The DHC runs from 1 to 5, and grade 5 is very great need, for example teeth unable to erupt or cleft lip and palate.

whyNot.0: Grade 1 means no need for treatment.
whyNot.1: Grade 3 is borderline or moderate need.
whyNot.3: There is no grade 10 in the DHC; 10 is the top of the Aesthetic Component.

C.q: Why are retainers fitted at the end of orthodontic treatment?
options: To stop the teeth drifting back
To keep moving teeth into place
To protect the enamel from acid
To widen the upper jaw further
C.why: Teeth tend to relapse towards their original positions, so retainers hold them where treatment left them.

whyNot.1: Active movement is finished by the time retainers are fitted.
whyNot.2: Retainers don't protect enamel; fluoride and diet do.
whyNot.3: Jaw expansion uses a different, active appliance.

C.q: The orthodontist asks you to pass the instrument to trim the ends of a newly placed archwire at the back of the mouth. Which do you pass?
C.why: Distal end cutters cut the archwire flush behind the last molar and hold the cut piece so it isn't dropped.

whyNot.0: Adams pliers adjust the clasps of removable appliances.
whyNot.1: A band pusher seats molar bands.
whyNot.3: A bracket holder places brackets onto the teeth.

reteach.title: IOTN is a two-question test
reteach.question: Imagine the orthodontist asks two questions about every patient: 'Is this bite a risk to their teeth?' and 'How much does it affect how they look?' How does IOTN answer each?

blocks.body: Question one is the Dental Health Component: a 1 to 5 grade based on the worst problem the orthodontist finds, such as a big overjet or a tooth stuck in the bone. Question two is the Aesthetic Component: the patient's smile is matched against 10 photos. Grades 4 and 5 qualify for NHS treatment on health alone. Grade 3 is borderline, so looks decide it: an AC of 6 or more tips it into NHS treatment.

blocks.h: Does an under-18 qualify for NHS treatment? (England)

blocks.text: DHC tops out at 5; AC tops out at 10. If an option mentions DHC 6 or higher, it is wrong.

explain.body: The DHC grades health need from 1 to 5 using the worst feature. The AC scores appearance from 1 to 10 using photographs. In England under-18s usually qualify with DHC 4 or 5, or DHC 3 plus AC 6 or more.

test.q: What does the IOTN Aesthetic Component use to score a patient?
options: A probe with a black band
test.why: The AC compares the patient's front teeth with 10 graded photographs.

whyNot.1: A probe with a black band is used for the BPE, a gum assessment.
whyNot.2: Counting decayed teeth is a caries measure, not IOTN.
whyNot.3: A lateral ceph shows jaw relationships but isn't how the AC is scored.

explain.body: Removable appliances tip teeth and are held with clasps. Fixed appliances bond brackets to the teeth and move them in every direction. Functional appliances guide jaw growth in growing children.

test.q: What holds a removable orthodontic appliance in place?
test.why: Removable appliances are held by wire clasps (such as Adams clasps) on the teeth.

whyNot.0: Bonded brackets are part of a fixed appliance.
whyNot.1: Cemented bands are part of a fixed appliance.
whyNot.2: An archwire runs through brackets on a fixed appliance.

explain.body: Plaque round brackets causes white spot lesions and gingivitis. Brush twice daily and after meals, use interdental brushes, fluoride toothpaste and a fluoride rinse if advised, and limit sugary drinks and sticky foods.

explain.caption: Plaque trapped near the gum line inflames the gingiva and demineralises enamel.

test.q: When should a patient using a fluoride mouthrinse during orthodontic treatment use it?
options: At a different time from brushing
Instead of brushing at lunchtime each day
test.why: Using the rinse at a different time, such as after lunch, adds an extra fluoride exposure rather than washing toothpaste fluoride away.

whyNot.0: Rinsing straight after brushing washes away the fluoride from the toothpaste.
whyNot.2: Bedtime is when the toothpaste is used; the rinse works best at another time.
whyNot.3: A rinse adds to brushing; it never replaces it.

explain.body: After the braces come off, retainers hold the teeth. They can be removable (clear vacuum-formed or Hawley) or a fixed wire bonded behind the front teeth. They are often worn long term.

test.q: A patient's bonded retainer wire has come loose from one tooth. What is the best advice?
options: Contact the practice for it to be checked
Pull the wire off and throw it away
Glue it back with a household adhesive
Leave it until the next routine check-up
test.why: A loose bonded retainer can let teeth move or catch the tongue, so it should be checked and repaired promptly.

whyNot.1: Removing it risks the teeth drifting back.
whyNot.2: Household glue is unsafe in the mouth and won't hold.
whyNot.3: Waiting allows relapse and the wire may cause injury.
